turns.doctor_question: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi Dr. Smith. Well, I'm here because I've been having a really hard time with my appearance. I teach high school, and whenever I have to look at myself on our recorded lesson videos, I just can't stop seeing this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face. 

It's really all I can focus on. And once I notice it, I just feel like... well, like my students, their parents, the other staff—everyone must just be staring right at it instead of actually listening to anything I'm saying.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes an intense preoccupation with a perceived defect in their facial appearance ('crooked, swollen-looking side of my face') stating it is all they can focus on.

turns.doctor_question: On a typical day, about how much time would you say you spend thinking about or checking on this part of your face?
turns.patient_response:
It's honestly hard to put an exact number of hours on it, but it takes up a massive part of my day. It's almost constant. 

Especially before I post a recorded lesson or join a parent conference... I just get stuck. I keep changing the camera angle to see if it looks less crooked, or I'll replay the video clips over and over. I even find myself just covering parts of my face with my hand while I'm on camera. Sometimes I end up re-recording a whole lesson so many times that I completely miss doing my prep work. It's actually gotten to the point where I'm ending up late to my classes because I can't stop checking and fixing it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient reports that thinking about and checking their perceived facial defect takes up a massive, almost constant part of their day.
symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient describes engaging in repetitive behaviors in response to appearance concerns, including repeatedly checking and changing camera angles, replaying video clips, covering their face with their hand, and re-recording lessons.

turns.doctor_question: When you think about how crooked or swollen that side of your face looks to you, do you think it's possible you might be overestimating how noticeable it is to other people, or do you feel certain that others see it exactly as severely as you do?
turns.patient_response: I... I mean, I guess it's possible I might be overestimating it a little bit? Like, maybe people aren't staring at it *every* single second. But... no, I really do think they see it. It's just so obvious to me. When I look in the mirror or at those videos, it's right there. It's crooked, it's swollen. I just don't see how anyone could miss it. So, even if I'm maybe making it a tiny bit worse in my head, I still feel pretty certain that everyone else is seeing the exact same flaw I am.
